title: Janaka, the king who was free
hookLine: a born hermit is sent to learn freedom from a king in a palace: the world is for experience and liberation
carry: bhoga and apavarga: the world is for both
tomorrow: two students look into the water for the self. only one goes back.

lines: A HERMIT SENT TO A KING.
cards: Shuka, the young sage who sat beside the dying Parikshit, wanted nothing from the world, the stories say, almost from birth. His father, Vyasa, sends him to learn about freedom anyway, and not from a hermit. From a king.
In the Mahabharata, Shuka walks to Mithila, to King Janaka. The guards make him wait at the gate. He doesn't mind.
Then he's led inside, into gardens, music and every comfort, and none of it moves him.

teach.h: IF MITHILA BURNS, NOTHING OF MINE BURNS.
teach.b: And then Janaka, a man with a kingdom to run, teaches him. Janaka is remembered in the Mahabharata for one line: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.
In the Gita, Krishna names him: Janaka and others reached perfection through action. A king, ruling, and free. Now Patanjali, sutra 2.18.
The seen, everything that can be watched, the mountains, the body, the mind itself, is made of light, activity and stillness, and it has a purpose: bhoga and apavarga.
Experience and liberation. The world is there so the seer can taste it, and so the seer can be free of the confusion. Both, not one instead of the other.
Sutra 2.21: the seen exists for the seer's sake. And 2.22 adds something tender: when one person is free, the world doesn't vanish.
It stays, shared with everyone still living in it. Janaka didn't walk away from his people; he kept ruling them. Hindu teaching makes room for this.
It names four aims of life side by side: dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation.
Not the world or freedom. Both. So, the week.
The passing taken for lasting. The power taken as mine. The pull and the push.
The clinging, even in the wise. Seeds that ripen. Fire fed with ghee.
And today, the turn: the same world that tangles you is the way through.

how: Hindu teaching names four aims of life, dharma, artha, kama and moksha, and Janaka of Mithila is the classic example of a householder king who was free. In the Samkhya and Yoga schools, nature is understood to exist for the sake of awareness, offering both experience and the chance of liberation; students study these sutras with the classical commentary.

o: liberation: the seer finally free of confusion
experience: the seer tasting the world
the end of the world when everyone is free

games.q: the king and the sutras — tap the pairs.
p: the world stays for everyone else

s: Patanjali says the seen world is an enemy to escape
2.18 gives it a purpose: experience and liberation.
Vyasa sent his son Shuka to learn about freedom from a king
in the Mahabharata, Shuka learns from King Janaka, in a palace.
when one person is free, the world stays for everyone else
2.22: it doesn't cease, because it is shared with others.

games.q: one seer finally sees clearly. its purpose is done. what happens to the world?
o: it no longer binds that seer, but stays for everyone else.
nothing changes, so the work was pointless.
games.why: 2.22: though it has ceased for the one whose purpose is done, it hasn't ceased, because it is common to others.

practice: First, experience: let one sense fill up, the sounds in the room or the light through your eyelids, and taste it fully without grabbing. Then freedom: notice that the sound comes and goes, and the hearing stays.
Move between the two, tasting and watching, as many times as you like.

wordCard.voice: Apavarga, release, liberation. In the Yoga Sutras, the seen exists for the seer, for two things: experience and liberation.

orig.note: Sanskrit apavarga: release, liberation; paired in 2.18 with bhoga, experience.

carryVoice: Your line: bhoga and apavarga, the world is for both: living and freedom. Janaka had a palace and was free. That's the week, day four hundred fifty-five.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Vyasa sends Shuka to King Janaka at Mithila; Janaka's saying 'if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns')
Bhagavad Gita 3.20 (Janaka and others reached perfection through action)
Yoga Sutra 2.18 (light, activity, stillness; experience and liberation)
Yoga Sutra 2.20–2.21 (the seer is pure seeing; the seen exists for its sake)
Yoga Sutra 2.22 (it does not cease, being common to others)
